lead: A real mixture usually differs from an ideal solution even at the same temperature, pressure and composition. The property change of mixing measures the whole change from pure components to mixture. The excess property measures only the part left after the ideal-solution change is removed. This split is useful because ideal mixing has a known entropy term, while real interactions add heat, volume change and activity coefficients. Distillation, solvent selection and heat-of-mixing calculations all need this split.
prereq: You need partial molar properties from partial molar properties, ideal solutions from ideal and non-ideal solutions, and G = H − TS.

blocks.text: For any molar property M of a mixture at fixed T and P, the property change of mixing is the mixture value minus the pure-component values weighted by mole fraction. Write it per mole of mixture.

blocks.where: ΔM<sub>mix</sub> is the change per mole of mixture when pure components mix; M is the mixture molar property; x<sub>i</sub> is mole fraction of component i; M<sub>i</sub><sup>pure</sup> is the molar property of pure i at the same T and P.

blocks.text: The same definition applies to U, H, S, G and V. For an ideal solution, ΔH<sub>mix</sub><sup>id</sup> = 0 because unlike contacts have the average energy of like contacts, and ΔV<sub>mix</sub><sup>id</sup> = 0 because the molecules are similar in size and pack the same way as in the pure liquids. Entropy and Gibbs energy still change because mixing increases randomness.

blocks.where: R is the gas constant, 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹; x<sub>i</sub> are mole fractions; ln is natural logarithm. Each ln x<sub>i</sub> is negative, so Σ x<sub>i</sub> ln x<sub>i</sub> is negative and ΔS<sub>mix</sub><sup>id</sup> is positive.

blocks.text: ΔG<sub>mix</sub><sup>id</sup> = RT Σ x<sub>i</sub> ln x<sub>i</sub>
blocks.where: T is absolute temperature in K. Each ln x<sub>i</sub> is negative, so ΔG<sub>mix</sub><sup>id</sup> is negative for spontaneous ideal mixing at fixed T and P.

blocks.text: A real mixture adds an excess part to each of these ideal changes. The excess part can be positive or negative.
An excess property is the real property change of mixing minus the ideal property change of mixing at the same T, P and composition.

blocks.where: M<sup>E</sup> is excess molar property; M<sup>id</sup> is the molar property of an ideal solution at the same T, P and x<sub>i</sub>. The superscript E means excess.

blocks.text: For enthalpy and volume, the ideal mixing terms are zero, so H<sup>E</sup> = ΔH<sub>mix</sub> and V<sup>E</sup> = ΔV<sub>mix</sub>. A positive H<sup>E</sup> means mixing absorbs heat. A negative H<sup>E</sup> means mixing releases heat. A positive V<sup>E</sup> means the mixture expands on mixing; a negative V<sup>E</sup> means contraction.
For Gibbs energy the ideal term is not zero. The excess Gibbs energy is linked to activity coefficients.
G<sup>E</sup> = RT Σ x<sub>i</sub> ln γ<sub>i</sub>
blocks.where: GE is excess molar Gibbs energy; γi is the activity coefficient of i from Chapter 5.7. For an ideal solution every γi = 1, so GE = 0.

blocks.text: Entropy follows from G<sup>E</sup> = H<sup>E</sup> − T S<sup>E</sup>. The excess entropy is S<sup>E</sup> = (H<sup>E</sup> − G<sup>E</sup>)/T. This relation lets you find one excess property if you know the other two at the same T, P and composition.
Activity coefficients come from the partial molar excess Gibbs energy, not from G<sup>E</sup> alone.

blocks.where: n is total moles; ni is moles of i; nj means other mole numbers held fixed. The derivative is partial molar. Chapter 5.8 builds models from this formula.

blocks.text: Excess properties are per mole of mixture unless stated otherwise. To get a total property change, multiply by total moles. If a table gives V<sup>E</sup> in cm³/mol, a 2.00 mol mixture has total excess volume 2.00 × V<sup>E</sup> cm³.

The figure uses V<sup>E</sup> = 2x<sub>1</sub>x<sub>2</sub> cm³/mol. At x<sub>1</sub> = 0.50, V<sup>E</sup> = 2 × 0.50 × 0.50 = 0.500 cm³/mol. For an ideal solution V<sup>E</sup> = 0, so the curve would sit on the zero line. The positive hump is expansion on mixing.

Some pairs contract on mixing and release heat; others expand and absorb heat. Use measured or model values when a heat or volume balance matters. For mixing at constant pressure with no shaft work, the heat that must be supplied to keep the temperature constant is Q = nΔH<sub>mix</sub> = nH<sup>E</sup>: positive for endothermic mixing, negative (heat to be removed) for exothermic mixing. Do not assume ideal behaviour just because the components look similar.

figure.caption: Left, the first example: the excess volume 2x₁x₂ peaks at 0.500 cm³/mol, while an ideal solution stays on zero. Right, the second example: the ideal Gibbs energy of mixing (−1679 J/mol) plus the excess Gibbs energy (+678 J/mol) gives ΔG of mixing = −1001 J/mol, so the liquids still mix.

examples.question: For a binary liquid at fixed T and P, V<sup>E</sup> = 2x<sub>1</sub>x<sub>2</sub> cm³/mol. At x<sub>1</sub> = 0.50, find ΔV<sub>mix</sub> per mole of mixture and the total ΔV<sub>mix</sub> for 2.00 mol of mixture.
steps: Total ΔV<sub>mix</sub> = n ΔV<sub>mix</sub> = 2.00 mol × 0.500 cm³/mol = 1.00 cm³.
examples.answer: ΔV<sub>mix</sub> = 0.500 cm³/mol, and the total change for 2.00 mol is 1.00 cm³.
examples.check:
x1 = 0.50
x2 = 1.0 - x1
VE = 2 * x1 * x2
dV_ideal = 0.0
dV_mix = VE + dV_ideal
n = 2.00
total = n * dV_mix
print(VE)
print(dV_mix)
print(total)

examples.question: At 300 K and 1 bar a binary liquid with x<sub>1</sub> = 0.40 has γ<sub>1</sub> = 1.60 and γ<sub>2</sub> = 1.15 (pure-liquid standard states) and a measured heat of mixing H<sup>E</sup> = +800 J/mol. Find G<sup>E</sup>, ΔG<sub>mix</sub>, S<sup>E</sup> and ΔS<sub>mix</sub>, and the heat needed to keep 5.0 mol of this mixture at 300 K as it forms.
steps: ΔG<sub>mix</sub> = ΔG<sub>mix</sub><sup>id</sup> + G<sup>E</sup> = −1679 + 678 = −1001 J/mol: still negative, so the liquids mix.
ΔS<sub>mix</sub><sup>id</sup> = −R Σ x<sub>i</sub> ln x<sub>i</sub> = 8.314 × 0.6730 = 5.60 J/(mol·K); ΔS<sub>mix</sub> = 5.60 + 0.41 = 6.00 J/(mol·K).
Heat: ΔH<sub>mix</sub> = H<sup>E</sup> = 800 J/mol, so Q = 5.0 × 800 = +4000 J must be supplied (mixing is endothermic).
Check: ΔG<sub>mix</sub> = ΔH<sub>mix</sub> − TΔS<sub>mix</sub> = 800 − 300 × 6.00 = −1000 J/mol, matching −1001 J/mol within rounding.
examples.answer: G<sup>E</sup> = 678 J/mol, ΔG<sub>mix</sub> = −1001 J/mol, S<sup>E</sup> = 0.41 J/(mol·K), ΔS<sub>mix</sub> = 6.00 J/(mol·K); 4.0 kJ of heat must be supplied for 5.0 mol.

traps: ΔM<sub>mix</sub> includes the ideal part; M<sup>E</sup> does not. Do not set M<sup>E</sup> = ΔM<sub>mix</sub> for S or G; that is true only for H, U and V.
Excess properties are per mole of mixture. Multiply by total moles for a vessel; do not add a per-mole value to a total mole value.
M<sup>E</sup> = ΔM<sub>mix</sub> − ΔM<sub>mix</sub><sup>id</sup>. Reversing the subtraction gives the wrong sign; a negative V<sup>E</sup> means contraction.
For ideal solutions ΔH<sub>mix</sub> and ΔV<sub>mix</sub> are zero, but ΔS<sub>mix</sub> and ΔG<sub>mix</sub> are not zero. Examiners often ask which ideal mixing changes vanish.
Activity coefficients come from the partial molar excess Gibbs energy, (∂(nG<sup>E</sup>)/∂n<sub>i</sub>), not from G<sup>E</sup> by a simple division.

quiz.q: Define ΔM<sub>mix</sub> and M<sup>E</sup> for a mixture at fixed T and P.
quiz.a: ΔM<sub>mix</sub> = M − Σx<sub>i</sub>M<sub>i</sub><sup>pure</sup> is the change per mole from pure components to mixture. M<sup>E</sup> = ΔM<sub>mix</sub> − ΔM<sub>mix</sub><sup>id</sup> is the part beyond ideal mixing.

quiz.q: Why are ΔH<sub>mix</sub><sup>id</sup> and ΔV<sub>mix</sub><sup>id</sup> zero for an ideal solution?
quiz.a: Unlike contacts have the average energy of like contacts, so no heat is released or absorbed; the molecules pack the same way as in the pure liquids, so volumes add. Mixing changes only entropy and Gibbs energy.

quiz.q: For V<sup>E</sup> = 3x<sub>1</sub>x<sub>2</sub> cm³/mol at x<sub>1</sub> = 0.25, find ΔV<sub>mix</sub> per mole and for 4.00 mol.
quiz.a: x<sub>2</sub> = 0.75. V<sup>E</sup> = 3 × 0.25 × 0.75 = 0.5625 cm³/mol. ΔV<sub>mix</sub><sup>id</sup> = 0, so ΔV<sub>mix</sub> = 0.5625 cm³/mol. Total = 4.00 × 0.5625 = 2.25 cm³.

quiz.q: G<sup>E</sup> = RTΣx<sub>i</sub>lnγ<sub>i</sub>. What does G<sup>E</sup> = 0 tell you about a solution at that composition?
quiz.a: It means Σx<sub>i</sub>lnγ<sub>i</sub> = 0. If all γ<sub>i</sub> = 1, the solution is ideal; more generally nonideal effects cancel in Gibbs energy, but H<sup>E</sup> or S<sup>E</sup> need not be zero.

quiz.q: For a binary mixture H<sup>E</sup> = −200 J/mol at x<sub>1</sub> = 0.5. Find ΔH<sub>mix</sub> for 3.00 mol.
quiz.a: ΔH<sub>mix</sub> = H<sup>E</sup> = −200 J/mol because ideal mixing enthalpy is zero. Total = 3.00 × (−200) = −600 J.

quiz.q: State one difference between ΔG<sub>mix</sub> and G<sup>E</sup>.
quiz.a: ΔG<sub>mix</sub> includes the ideal entropy of mixing plus the nonideal part. G<sup>E</sup> removes the ideal part and is zero for an ideal solution.

quiz.q: Why is G<sup>E</sup> used to obtain activity coefficients instead of ΔG<sub>mix</sub>?
quiz.a: The ideal part of ΔG<sub>mix</sub> has a known composition dependence. Removing it leaves G<sup>E</sup>, whose partial molar derivative gives lnγ<sub>i</sub> directly; using ΔG<sub>mix</sub> would mix ideal and nonideal contributions.

beyond: Not for the exam. Excess properties lead to group-contribution models such as UNIFAC and to predictive models such as COSMO-RS, used when data are missing. Plant energy balances use heats of mixing. Search next: excess Gibbs energy models, UNIFAC, enthalpy of mixing measurement.
